idiom_name: []T value slices with index handles (parallel slices for struct-of-arrays)
implementation_notes: Slices are descriptors over a contiguous backing array (pointer, length, capacity) and arrays are values, so the idiomatic Go realization is the packed one: keep records in []T, pass them by value, and reference them by index instead of by *T. What replaces the classic structure: value slices plus indices replace graphs of pointers, so there is no per-record allocation, the collector has fewer pointers to trace, and the loop is one contiguous scan that the compiler can bounds-check-hoist. slices (Go 1.21) supplies the generic upkeep - slices.SortFunc/DeleteFunc/SortStableFunc to reorder by a hot field or compact the active prefix. Struct-of-arrays (separate []float32 per field, or a struct of slices) is the columnar variant when a loop reads only some fields.
pitfalls: []*T or []any reintroduces indirection: each element is a pointer (or an interface with a type word) to a separately allocated value, so the scan becomes pointer chasing again.
append may reallocate and copy the backing array, so any *T or unsafe.Pointer taken earlier becomes stale; keep indices or preallocate with make([]T, 0, n) and never keep element addresses.
The collector does not move heap objects, but a slice header copied to another goroutine still shares the same backing array - concurrent writers need per-shard slices or explicit synchronisation.
Interface-typed elements also box on assignment and force two-word elements, doubling the bytes each cache line must carry.
